mints.struck: Everything: the first and the main US mint.
mints.note: Philadelphia coins carried no mark for most of history. P appears on the 1942-1945 war nickels, then on nickels, dimes and quarters from 1980, and on cents from 2017.

mints.struck: Coins for circulation, and collector sets.
mints.note: The Denver mint opened in 1906. Its D appears on cents from 1911.

mints.struck: Coins for circulation until 1974, and since then proof coins for collectors.
mints.note: No mint marks were used from 1965 to 1967, so no S from those years. Today the S marks proof coins.

mints.struck: Gold and silver bullion coins, commemoratives and some collector coins; a few circulating coins.
mints.note: West Point has been a full mint since 1988. Its W is a rare find in change: the 2019 quarter with a W is an example.

mints.struck: Silver and gold coins from the Comstock silver mines.
mints.note: Short-lived and small, so a CC coin is prized by collectors. It struck silver and gold only, never cents or nickels.

mints.struck: Gold and silver coins, including many Morgan silver dollars.
mints.note: It closed in 1861 when the Civil War began, and reopened in 1879. You will not find an O on a coin in your pocket today.
Struck from local gold. It closed in 1861.
Another branch of the 1830s gold rush, in Georgia. Its D is not Denver's: look at the date to tell them apart.

eras.where: On the front, under the date. A cent with no mark came from Philadelphia until 2017.
On the back, to the right of the Monticello building. The 1942-1945 war nickels have a large mark above the dome instead.
On the front, near the date. No marks were used in 1965, 1966 and 1967.
